title: How to study this phase: from zero to writing a paper
tagline: Seven stages. Do them in order; each one only uses what came before.
explain:
**The path** (the sidebar follows exactly this order):

1. **Foundations** - vectors/matrices, derivatives and gradient descent, probability. No prior math assumed beyond school algebra.
2. **Classical ML** - linear and logistic regression, trees and ensembles, kNN/SVM/Naive Bayes, clustering. These are still the strongest baselines on tabular data and the language reviewers use.
3. **Evaluation** - splits, cross-validation, metrics, leakage. Learn this *before* trusting any number.
4. **Neural networks** - perceptron, MLP, activations, how they train.
5. **Math deepening** - SVD, backprop in full, optimization theory, MLE/MAP, information theory, generalization theory.
6. **Modern ML** - attention/transformers, scaling laws, self-supervised, generative models, RL, Bayesian deep learning.
7. **Research craft** - statistics for papers, reading papers, experiment design, writing for IEEE/ISI.

**How to study each concept**: (a) read "How it works" and play with the interactive lab until you can predict what a slider will do; (b) derive the formula by hand on paper; (c) answer the interviewer/reviewer questions out loud; (d) implement it in 20-40 lines of NumPy; (e) tick "Mark understood" only after (b)-(d).

**Milestones**: after stage 3 you can build and honestly evaluate a classical model on a dataset. After stage 5 you can read most ML papers' Methods sections. After stage 7 you can design, run and write up an experiment worth submitting.

**Suggested pace** (part-time): stages 1-2 ~4 weeks, 3-4 ~2 weeks, 5 ~4 weeks, 6 ~4 weeks, 7 ongoing alongside a real project.

**Where the rest of the curriculum lives.** This phase teaches the mathematical and conceptual core and ends with a *Complete math reference* group that lists every topic of the university syllabus (linear algebra, calculus, probability, statistics, optimisation). The algorithm catalogue continues in the next phases: **Classical ML** (Python stack, preprocessing, every regression/classification/clustering/dimensionality-reduction/association algorithm, ensembles, learning theory, tuning, metrics), **Advanced ML + RL** (kernels, EM, HMM/CRF, graphical models, metaheuristics, causal/federated/transfer/online/meta-learning, reinforcement learning), **Deep Learning**, and **Research Methods** (PRISMA, statistical tests, paper writing, the 18-month plan).
tradeoffs: Going deep on theory first feels productive but delays intuition; alternate: one theory concept, one coding exercise.
Skipping classical ML to jump to transformers leaves gaps in evaluation and baselines that reviewers notice.
pitfalls: Watching lectures without deriving or coding anything.
Collecting papers instead of reproducing one.
Skipping the Evaluation stage and trusting leaderboard numbers.
interview: How would you explain gradient descent to a non-technical person?
What baseline would you run before a neural network on tabular data?
use: Treat as the syllabus; revisit the order if you already know a stage and simply tick its items.
avoid: Do not start at stage 6 because it is exciting; the gaps will show in every derivation.

title: Vectors, matrices and shapes (from zero)
tagline: Data, weights and embeddings are all arrays. Learn dot products and shapes and half of ML is readable.
explain:
A **vector** is a list of numbers, e.g. a house described by $x=[\text{area},\text{rooms},\text{age}]$. You can picture it as an arrow or a point. A **matrix** is a table of numbers; a dataset with $n$ examples and $d$ features is an $n\times d$ matrix $X$.

**Operations you need**
- Add / scale: component-wise. $2x$ doubles every entry.
- **Dot product**: $a\cdot b=\sum_i a_ib_i=\|a\|\|b\|\cos\theta$. Big when the vectors point the same way, 0 when perpendicular.
- **Norm** (length): $\|x\|_2=\sqrt{\sum x_i^2}$; $\|x\|_1=\sum|x_i|$.
- **Cosine similarity**: $\cos\theta=\dfrac{a\cdot b}{\|a\|\|b\|}$ - compares direction, ignores length (why it is used for text embeddings).
- **Matrix-vector product**: $y=Wx$ means each output is a dot product of one row of $W$ with $x$. A neural-network layer is exactly this plus a bias and a nonlinearity.

**Shapes are the #1 debugging tool**: $(m\times n)\cdot(n\times p)=(m\times p)$; the inner dimensions must match. Write shapes next to every equation. Broadcasting in NumPy/PyTorch silently expands size-1 dimensions - powerful and a classic source of bugs.

**Matrices as transformations**: a matrix stretches, rotates or squashes space. Use the lab above: change the numbers and watch the unit circle change. A matrix whose determinant is 0 squashes space onto a line - information is lost and it cannot be inverted.
tradeoffs: Vectorised matrix code is 100x faster than Python loops but hides shapes - assert shapes.
Cosine similarity ignores magnitude, which sometimes carries information (e.g. confidence).
pitfalls: Row vs column vector confusion: $x^\top y$ vs $xy^\top$ (scalar vs matrix).
Broadcasting a (n,) array against (n,1) and getting an (n,n) result.
Comparing embeddings with dot product when they are not normalised.
interview: What does a dot product measure?
What is the shape of the output of a linear layer with input (batch, 512) and 256 units?
Why cosine and not Euclidean distance for text embeddings?
use: Reading every formula in ML; implementing layers and similarity search.
avoid: Do not hand-write loops over examples when a matrix product does it.

qa.q: Compute the cosine similarity of [1,2] and [2,4].
qa.a: $a\cdot b=2+8=10$, $\|a\|=\sqrt5$, $\|b\|=\sqrt{20}$, so $\cos\theta=10/(\sqrt5\sqrt{20})=10/10=1$: same direction, different length.

deep.title: Exercise ladder
deep.body: 1. Multiply a (2x3) by a (3x2) matrix by hand. 2. Verify (AB)^T = B^T A^T numerically. 3. Write cosine similarity in one NumPy line. 4. Implement a dense layer forward pass and check every shape.

title: Derivatives, gradients and gradient descent (from zero)
tagline: A derivative is a slope; learning is walking downhill on a loss surface.
explain:
The **derivative** $f'(x)$ is the slope of $f$ at $x$: how much $f$ changes per tiny change in $x$. Rules: $(x^n)'=nx^{n-1}$, $(e^x)'=e^x$, $(\ln x)'=1/x$, sum rule, product rule, and the **chain rule** $\dfrac{d}{dx}f(g(x))=f'(g(x))\,g'(x)$ - the engine of backpropagation.

With many inputs, the **gradient** $\nabla f=[\partial f/\partial x_1,\dots,\partial f/\partial x_d]$ is the vector of slopes; it points in the direction of steepest *increase*. A **partial derivative** treats the other variables as constants.

**Gradient descent**: to minimise a loss $L(\theta)$ repeat

```math
\theta\leftarrow\theta-\eta\,\nabla L(\theta)
```

where $\eta$ is the **learning rate**. Too small: slow. Too large: overshoots and may diverge. On a non-convex curve it can stop in a local minimum or at a flat saddle - use the lab: change the start point and the learning rate.

**Worked example**: $L(w)=(w-3)^2$. $L'(w)=2(w-3)$. Start $w=0$, $\eta=0.1$: $w_1=0-0.1\cdot(-6)=0.6$, $w_2=0.6-0.1\cdot(-4.8)=1.08$, ... converging to 3. At $\eta=1$ it oscillates between 0 and 6 forever; at $\eta>1$ it diverges.

**Stochastic** gradient descent uses a random minibatch to estimate the gradient - noisy but cheap, and the noise often helps escape poor regions.
tradeoffs: Larger learning rate = faster but riskier; schedules start high and decay.
Full-batch gradients are exact but expensive; minibatches trade accuracy for speed.
pitfalls: Moving *with* the gradient instead of against it (sign error).
Forgetting to rescale the loss/inputs - badly scaled features make descent crawl.
Assuming a zero gradient means a minimum (could be a maximum or saddle).
interview: Explain gradient descent in two sentences.
What happens if the learning rate is too high or too low?
Compute the gradient of $(wx-y)^2$ with respect to $w$.
use: Understanding every training loop; debugging divergence or slow training.
avoid: Do not tune learning rate by feel alone - run a learning-rate sweep on a log scale.

qa.a: Let $e=wx+b-y$. By the chain rule $\partial L/\partial w=2e\,x$ and $\partial L/\partial b=2e$.

deep.title: Exercise ladder
deep.body: 1. Differentiate f(x)=x^2 e^x by hand. 2. Implement gradient descent for (w-3)^2 and plot w vs step for 3 learning rates. 3. Verify your gradient with a finite difference (f(x+h)-f(x-h))/2h.

title: Probability and statistics basics (from zero)
tagline: Randomness, averages, spread, conditional probability and why averages of many things become predictable.
explain:
**Probability** assigns a number in $[0,1]$ to events. A **random variable** $X$ maps outcomes to numbers; its **distribution** says how likely each value is (a PMF for discrete, a density/PDF for continuous).

- **Mean (expectation)** $\mathbb E[X]=\sum x\,p(x)$ - the long-run average.
- **Variance** $\mathrm{Var}(X)=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E X)^2]$ and **standard deviation** $\sigma=\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}}$ - typical spread.
- **Joint / marginal / conditional**: $P(A\mid B)=P(A\cap B)/P(B)$. **Independence**: $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$.
- **Bayes' rule**: $P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{P(B\mid A)P(A)}{P(B)}$.

**Worked Bayes example**: a disease affects 1% of people; a test is 95% sensitive and 90% specific. If you test positive, $P(\text{sick}\mid +)=\dfrac{0.95\cdot0.01}{0.95\cdot0.01+0.10\cdot0.99}\approx0.088$. Only ~9%! The base rate matters - the classic reason accuracy alone misleads.

**Key distributions**: Bernoulli (coin), Binomial, **Gaussian** $\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ (68-95-99.7 rule), Uniform, Poisson (counts), Exponential. **Law of large numbers**: the sample mean converges to the true mean. **Central limit theorem**: sums/averages of many independent variables look Gaussian regardless of the original distribution - why the Gaussian is everywhere and why confidence intervals work.

**Sample vs population**: we only see a sample. The unbiased sample variance divides by $n-1$, not $n$ (Bessel's correction).
tradeoffs: Assuming Gaussian data makes maths easy but heavy tails (income, latency) break mean/variance based reasoning.
More samples shrink standard error as $1/\sqrt n$ - halving it needs 4x the data.
pitfalls: Base-rate neglect (ignoring $P(A)$ in Bayes).
Confusing $P(A|B)$ with $P(B|A)$ (prosecutor's fallacy).
Treating correlated samples as independent.
Using the mean for heavy-tailed data instead of the median/quantiles.
interview: Why is a 95%-accurate test often mostly wrong when positive?
What does the CLT say and why does it matter?
Why divide by n-1 for the sample variance?
use: Evaluation, A/B tests, uncertainty, every probabilistic loss later.
avoid: Do not report a mean without a spread (std/CI).

qa.q: Two fair dice: probability the sum is 7?

deep.title: Exercise ladder
deep.body: 1. Simulate 10,000 dice-sum experiments and compare with the exact distribution. 2. Sample means of an exponential distribution for n=1,5,50 - plot the histograms and watch the CLT. 3. Reproduce the 8.8% Bayes result by simulation.

title: Linear regression: least squares, normal equation, ridge and lasso
tagline: The simplest model, and the template for almost everything: model, loss, optimise, regularise.
explain:
**Model**: $\hat y=w^\top x+b$. **Loss** (mean squared error): $L(w)=\tfrac1n\sum_i(w^\top x_i-y_i)^2=\tfrac1n\|Xw-y\|^2$ (absorb $b$ as a constant feature).

**Two ways to solve**
- **Closed form (normal equation)**: set $\nabla L=0\Rightarrow X^\top Xw=X^\top y\Rightarrow w^*=(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y$. Costs $O(nd^2+d^3)$; fails when features are collinear ($X^\top X$ singular).
- **Gradient descent**: $w\leftarrow w-\eta\,\tfrac2n X^\top(Xw-y)$. Scales to huge data; convex so it reaches the global optimum.

**Geometry**: $Xw^*$ is the orthogonal projection of $y$ onto the column space of $X$; the residual is perpendicular to every feature.

**Regularisation** fights overfitting (see the bias-variance lab, raise the degree then add $\lambda$):
- **Ridge (L2)**: $\min\|Xw-y\|^2+\lambda\|w\|^2\Rightarrow w=(X^\top X+\lambda I)^{-1}X^\top y$ - always invertible, shrinks weights.
- **Lasso (L1)**: $+\lambda\|w\|_1$ - drives some weights to exactly 0 (feature selection) because the L1 ball has corners.
- **Elastic net**: both.

**Assumptions for inference** (matter for papers): linearity, independent errors, constant variance (homoscedasticity), roughly normal residuals, no strong multicollinearity. Metrics: MSE, RMSE, MAE, $R^2=1-\dfrac{\sum(y-\hat y)^2}{\sum(y-\bar y)^2}$.

**Probabilistic view**: least squares is the maximum-likelihood estimate under Gaussian noise; ridge is MAP with a Gaussian prior.
tradeoffs: Interpretable and fast, but only captures linear relations (add polynomial/interaction features or move to trees/NNs).
Ridge keeps all features (stable); lasso selects features but is unstable when features are correlated.
pitfalls: Not scaling features before ridge/lasso/GD - penalty and convergence depend on scale.
Extrapolating far outside the training range.
High $R^2$ on training data with many features (adjusted $R^2$/validation instead).
Leaving outliers: squared loss is sensitive - consider Huber/MAE.
interview: Derive the normal equation.
Why does L1 produce sparsity and L2 does not?
What happens if two features are perfectly correlated?
use: Strong baseline, interpretable effects, small tabular data, quick sanity check for any regression problem.
avoid: Do not use plain least squares with more features than examples without regularisation.

qa.a: $L=\|Xw-y\|^2=w^\top X^\top Xw-2y^\top Xw+y^\top y$. $\nabla L=2X^\top Xw-2X^\top y=0\Rightarrow X^\top Xw=X^\top y$.

deep.title: Exercise ladder
deep.body: 1. Fit a line with np.linalg.lstsq and by gradient descent; compare. 2. Add 30 noise features and watch test error; fix with ridge. 3. Use lasso on a dataset and list the surviving features. 4. Derive ridge as MAP with a Gaussian prior.

title: Logistic regression and classification
tagline: Linear model + sigmoid + cross-entropy: the template for every classifier head.
explain:
For binary labels $y\in\{0,1\}$ model the probability: $P(y=1\mid x)=\sigma(w^\top x+b)$, $\sigma(z)=\dfrac{1}{1+e^{-z}}$. The quantity $z$ is the **log-odds**: $\log\frac{p}{1-p}=w^\top x+b$, so each weight is a change in log-odds per unit feature.

**Loss**: maximum likelihood gives binary cross-entropy $L=-\tfrac1n\sum[y\log p+(1-y)\log(1-p)]$. It is convex in $w$. Its gradient is beautifully simple:

```math
\nabla_wL=\tfrac1n X^\top(p-y)
```

The **decision boundary** $w^\top x+b=0$ is a hyperplane; the threshold (default 0.5) trades precision for recall. Multi-class: **softmax** regression with $p_k=\mathrm{softmax}(W x)_k$ and categorical cross-entropy (try the softmax lab).

**Why not MSE for classification?** With a sigmoid it gives non-convex loss and vanishing gradients when confidently wrong; cross-entropy does not.

**Regularise** with L2 (default in scikit-learn, $C=1/\lambda$). **Separable data**: without regularisation weights grow to infinity. **Class imbalance**: use class weights, resampling, or threshold tuning; judge by PR-AUC rather than accuracy.
tradeoffs: Well-calibrated, fast and interpretable but linear in the features.
Threshold choice is a business decision, not a modelling one.
pitfalls: Reporting accuracy on imbalanced data.
Perfect separation causing diverging coefficients.
Unscaled features slowing convergence.
Interpreting coefficients as causal.
interview: Derive the gradient of logistic loss.
Why is it a linear classifier although it has a sigmoid?
How do you choose the threshold?
use: Baseline classifier, risk scores, calibrated probabilities, final layer of neural nets.
avoid: Do not expect it to learn XOR-like interactions without feature engineering.

deep.title: Exercise ladder
deep.body: 1. Implement logistic regression with gradient descent in NumPy. 2. Plot the decision boundary on 2-D blobs. 3. Move the threshold and plot the precision-recall tradeoff. 4. Make the classes 95/5 imbalanced and compare accuracy to PR-AUC.

title: Decision trees, random forests and gradient boosting
tagline: The dominant family for tabular data: know how splits are chosen and why ensembles win.
explain:
A **decision tree** recursively splits the data with axis-aligned questions ("age < 30?"). At each node choose the split that most reduces **impurity**:

```math
\text{Gini}=1-\sum_k p_k^2,\qquad H=-\sum_k p_k\log_2 p_k,\qquad \text{Gain}=I(\text{parent})-\sum_{c}\tfrac{n_c}{n}I(c)
```

(regression trees minimise variance/MSE in each leaf). Leaves predict the majority class or mean. A single deep tree **overfits** (low bias, high variance); limit depth, min samples per leaf, or prune.

**Bagging / Random Forest**: train many trees on bootstrap samples, with a random subset of features at each split, and average. Averaging $B$ de-correlated high-variance trees cuts variance by up to $1/B$ without raising bias. Free validation: **out-of-bag** error.

**Gradient boosting** (XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost): build trees *sequentially*, each fitting the **negative gradient** (pseudo-residuals) of the loss at the current ensemble: $F_m=F_{m-1}+\eta\,h_m$, with $h_m\approx-\partial L/\partial F$. For squared loss that is literally fitting the residuals. Key knobs: number of trees, learning rate $\eta$ (small + more trees is better), depth (3-8), subsampling, L1/L2 on leaf weights, early stopping on validation.

**Why they win on tabular data**: handle mixed types and missing values, invariant to monotonic feature scaling, capture interactions automatically, need little preprocessing.
tradeoffs: Forest: robust, hard to overfit, parallel. Boosting: higher accuracy but needs tuning and early stopping, sequential.
Trees cannot extrapolate beyond the training range and are piecewise-constant.
pitfalls: Deep unpruned single tree as the 'final' model.
Impurity-based feature importance is biased toward high-cardinality features - use permutation importance/SHAP.
Target leakage through ID-like or future features.
Tuning boosting without early stopping.
interview: How does a tree choose a split?
Bagging vs boosting: bias/variance view?
Why prefer gradient boosting over a neural net for tabular data?
use: Tabular prediction, feature interactions, fast strong baselines, Kaggle-style problems.
avoid: Do not use trees for images/text/raw signals or when extrapolation is required.

qa.q: Why does random forest sample features at each split?
qa.a: To de-correlate the trees. Averaging variance is $\rho\sigma^2+\frac{1-\rho}{B}\sigma^2$; reducing the correlation $\rho$ between trees lowers the floor that more trees cannot go below.

deep.title: Exercise ladder
deep.body: 1. Compute Gini gain for a split by hand. 2. Fit a tree at depth 1..20 and plot train/validation accuracy. 3. Compare RandomForest vs LightGBM with early stopping on a tabular dataset. 4. Get permutation importance and compare with impurity importance.

title: k-NN, SVM, Naive Bayes: three different ideas
tagline: Instance-based, margin-based and generative classifiers - and when each is the right baseline.
explain:
**k-Nearest Neighbours**: predict by majority/mean of the $k$ closest training points. No training, all cost at prediction time; needs a good distance (scale features!) and suffers in high dimensions (distances concentrate - the curse of dimensionality). Small $k$ = high variance, large $k$ = high bias.

**Support Vector Machine**: choose the hyperplane that maximises the **margin** $2/\|w\|$. Soft-margin objective with hinge loss:

```math
\min_{w,b}\ \tfrac12\|w\|^2+C\sum_i\max\big(0,\,1-y_i(w^\top x_i+b)\big)
```

Only **support vectors** (points on/inside the margin) matter. The **kernel trick** replaces $x^\top x'$ by $k(x,x')$ (RBF $e^{-\gamma\|x-x'\|^2}$) to get nonlinear boundaries without computing the features. $C$: large = fit training data hard (overfit); $\gamma$: large = very local boundaries.

**Naive Bayes**: Bayes' rule with the "naive" assumption that features are independent given the class: $P(y\mid x)\propto P(y)\prod_jP(x_j\mid y)$. Train by counting; very fast, works well for text (bag of words) and small data despite the false assumption; use Laplace smoothing for unseen words.

**Choosing**: kNN as a quick non-parametric baseline and for retrieval; SVM on small/medium, high-dimensional data (text, genomics); Naive Bayes for a very fast text baseline.
tradeoffs: SVM kernel training is $O(n^2$-$n^3)$ - does not scale past ~100k samples; linear SVM does.
Naive Bayes probabilities are poorly calibrated though rankings are often good.
pitfalls: No feature scaling for kNN/SVM.
Tuning $C,\gamma$ on the test set - use cross-validation.
kNN in hundreds of dimensions without dimensionality reduction.
Zero probabilities in Naive Bayes without smoothing.
interview: Explain the margin and support vectors.
What is the kernel trick?
Why does Naive Bayes work despite the independence assumption being false?
use: Small/medium datasets, text baselines, nearest-neighbour retrieval ideas that lead to vector search.
avoid: Do not use kernel SVM on millions of rows.

qa.q: What does the curse of dimensionality do to kNN?
qa.a: In high dimensions the ratio of nearest to farthest distance approaches 1, so 'nearest' stops being meaningful; you need far more data, feature selection or learned embeddings.

deep.title: Exercise ladder
deep.body: 1. kNN from scratch with NumPy; plot error vs k. 2. SVM with RBF: grid-search C and gamma with cross-validation. 3. Naive Bayes spam filter with smoothing.

title: Unsupervised learning: k-means, GMM/EM, PCA, DBSCAN
tagline: Find structure without labels - and learn the EM algorithm that reappears in latent-variable models.
explain:
**k-means** minimises within-cluster variance $\sum_k\sum_{x\in C_k}\|x-\mu_k\|^2$ by alternating (1) assign each point to the nearest centroid, (2) set each centroid to the mean of its points (Lloyd's algorithm). Each step cannot increase the objective, so it converges - but only to a *local* optimum; use k-means++ initialisation and several restarts. It assumes roughly spherical, equally sized clusters and needs $k$ (elbow, silhouette score, gap statistic).

**Gaussian mixture model + EM**: $p(x)=\sum_k\pi_k\mathcal N(x\mid\mu_k,\Sigma_k)$. **E-step**: responsibilities $r_{ik}=\dfrac{\pi_k\mathcal N(x_i|\mu_k,\Sigma_k)}{\sum_j\pi_j\mathcal N(x_i|\mu_j,\Sigma_j)}$. **M-step**: re-estimate $\pi,\mu,\Sigma$ using $r_{ik}$ as soft counts. k-means is the hard-assignment, equal-spherical-variance limit of GMM. EM maximises a lower bound on the log-likelihood each iteration - the same idea as the VAE's ELBO.

**PCA** (dimensionality reduction): project onto the top-$k$ eigenvectors of the covariance matrix (see the linear-algebra concept); choose $k$ by explained variance. **t-SNE/UMAP** are for visualisation only - distances and cluster sizes in the plot are not reliable.

**DBSCAN**: density-based; core points have $\ge$ minPts neighbours within radius $\varepsilon$; finds arbitrary shapes and flags noise, no $k$ needed, but struggles with varying density.

**Evaluating without labels**: silhouette score $s=\dfrac{b-a}{\max(a,b)}$, Davies-Bouldin; better: downstream task performance or stability across resamples.
tradeoffs: k-means is fast and simple but rigid; GMM gives soft, elliptical clusters at higher cost; DBSCAN finds shapes but needs tuning of $\varepsilon$.
PCA is linear and interpretable; non-linear methods preserve local structure but distort global distances.
pitfalls: Not scaling features before k-means.
Interpreting t-SNE cluster distances/sizes.
Choosing $k$ only by the elbow without checking stability.
Running k-means on categorical data.
interview: Walk through the EM algorithm for a GMM.
How do you choose k?
How are PCA and SVD related?
use: Customer segmentation, anomaly detection, compression, visualisation, initialising or analysing embeddings.
avoid: Do not present unsupervised clusters as 'ground truth' categories.

qa.a: Each assignment step and each mean-update step can only decrease (or keep) the objective, which is bounded below, and there are finitely many assignments - so it converges, but to a local minimum.

deep.title: Exercise ladder
deep.body: 1. Implement k-means in 25 lines of NumPy; compare with 1 vs 10 restarts. 2. Fit a GMM with EM and plot soft assignments. 3. PCA of MNIST to 2-D and 50-D; measure explained variance. 4. DBSCAN on two-moons vs k-means.

title: Evaluation protocol: splits, cross-validation, tuning and leakage
tagline: The most common source of wrong results in papers and projects.
tradeoffs: More folds = less bias but more compute and higher variance of the estimate.
A held-out test set is clean but wastes data; CV uses data efficiently but is easier to leak.
pitfalls: Preprocessing on the full dataset before CV.
Random split of time-ordered data.
Reporting the best CV score after trying hundreds of configs as the expected performance.
Ignoring group structure.
interview: Why must the scaler be fit only on the training fold?
When do you use nested cross-validation?
How do you split time-series data?
use: Every experiment you will ever report.
avoid: Do not tune on the test set, ever - even 'just once to check'.

qa.a: Likely leakage or distribution shift: preprocessing before the split, duplicates/groups across folds, future data in features, or the production population differs from the training sample. Audit the pipeline, split by group/time, and compare feature distributions.

deep.title: Exercise ladder
deep.body: 1. Build a scikit-learn Pipeline (impute -> scale -> model) and run stratified 5-fold CV. 2. Deliberately leak (scale before split) and measure the optimism. 3. Plot learning curves for a tree and a linear model.

title: Neural networks from scratch: perceptron, MLP, activations, training loop
tagline: Stack linear layers with nonlinearities; train with backprop + gradient descent.
explain:
A **neuron** computes $a=\phi(w^\top x+b)$. A **layer** does it for many neurons at once: $a=\phi(Wx+b)$. An **MLP** stacks layers: $\hat y=W_3\,\phi(W_2\,\phi(W_1x+b_1)+b_2)+b_3$. Without the nonlinearity $\phi$ any depth collapses to one linear map ($W_3W_2W_1x$).

**Activations**: sigmoid $\sigma$ (saturates, gradient $\le0.25$), tanh, **ReLU** $\max(0,z)$ (cheap, no saturation for $z>0$, but "dying ReLU"), GELU/SiLU (smooth, used in transformers), softmax (output layer for classes).

**Universal approximation**: a wide enough one-hidden-layer network can approximate any continuous function on a compact set - but it says nothing about how to *find* the weights or how many neurons are needed; depth gives exponentially more efficient representations for compositional functions.

**Training loop** (every deep learning codebase):

```
for epoch:
    for batch in data:
        pred = model(x)              # forward
        loss = loss_fn(pred, y)
        loss.backward()              # backprop: gradients via the chain rule
        optimizer.step()             # update weights
        optimizer.zero_grad()
```

**Initialisation** matters (He/Xavier keep activations and gradients at stable scale); **normalisation** layers and **residual connections** make deep nets trainable; **dropout** and weight decay regularise. Use the backprop lab to see forward values and backward gradients on one neuron, then scale up in your head: the same local rule is applied at every node.
tradeoffs: MLPs are flexible but data-hungry and less competitive than trees on small tabular data.
Depth increases expressiveness and difficulty of optimisation.
pitfalls: Forgetting the nonlinearity.
All-zero or too-large initialisation (symmetry / exploding signals).
Not shuffling data; not normalising inputs.
Evaluating with dropout still on (forgetting model.eval()).
interview: Why do we need nonlinear activations?
Why does ReLU help versus sigmoid?
Walk through one training step.
use: Learning representations on images/text/signals; the base for everything in the modern-ML stage.
avoid: Do not reach for a deep net before a tuned gradient-boosting baseline on small tabular data.

qa.q: Can a single perceptron learn XOR?
qa.a: No - XOR is not linearly separable. One hidden layer with two nonlinear units solves it, which is the classic motivation for hidden layers.

deep.title: Exercise ladder
deep.body: 1. Implement a 2-layer MLP with manual backprop in NumPy and train it on XOR then on two-moons. 2. Gradient-check it. 3. Re-implement in PyTorch and compare. 4. Break it: remove the nonlinearity, set LR=10, zero-init - describe each failure.
